comments: As a very long time user and lover of SketchUp, I'm still peeved about the direction Trimble took in neglecting the SketchUp desktop modeler in favor of a web-based UI. Their licensing was also terrible... first they discontinued the free version of SketchUp, and then later on they discontinued perpetual licensing, meaning the only way to get the desktop modeler was to pay several hundred per year, which wasn't worth it to me. A modeler with SketchUp's incredible UI that can take full advantage of any computer's available graphics hardware to render large amounts of geometry more efficiently would be a wonderful thing.I'm very possessive of my SketchUp models, and so the idea of storing them on any kind of cloud server I don't have control over is abhorrent to me. There is a trick. Sign up with them, configure custom domain, but don’t set your MX records. On your MTA, route mail that goes to Outlook/Hotmail to go through their MSA with your Outlook credentials and headers stripped as if submitted directly by user. Outlook gets mail through their own MSA it trusts, rest of the world talks to your mail system directly. Replies still go to your MXes.I haven’t productionized this setup (I send maybe a dozen emails a year) but it worked for me ad hoc a couple years back, when I had to send a mail to an Outlook-hosted address and they blackholed everything I tried to send while 250 OKing me.reply

first_paragraph: By Thomas A. Johnson · Founder & CEO, MailRouteSince November 5, 2026, Microsoft's consumer mail service has been turning away some of the email from domains that don't publish a DMARC record. If your company emails customers, vendors or applicants with outlook.com, hotmail.com, live.com or msn.com addresses, some of that mail may be bouncing right now. Nobody announced it. The fix is one DNS record.Key takeawaysThe sender gets a bounce like this one, followed by a bracketed server name and ID that differ per message:On the first day, the same rejection came back without the (AS9031519) code:The wording suggests something is badly broken. Usually it isn't. The domains we have seen bounced mostly had working SPF, and many had DKIM too. What they were missing was the DMARC record that ties the two to the From address.Microsoft does have published sender rules. Since May 2025, domains that send more than 5,000 messages a day to Outlook.com have had to pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC, or get 550

title: I'm not convinced the AI bubble exists (matteoraso.github.io)
comments: Other than the fact that we’re due for one, this one is differently shaped in that there isn’t really widespread “irrational exuberance” and constant reporting about AI fortunes. I think your general investor is quite skeptical about AI and worries about exposure in their portfolio. Sure there is plenty of irrationality happening, but there is also a lot of real growth and changes in assumptions. Like the job market is way stronger than expected for even AI-threatened sectors (not entirely and I’m sorry if this affects your circles) but like we’re really just getting started here. I don’t think AI in today’s form will be the same as this time next year and that real growth is just beginning. All of the destruction of value that PE has wrought will only serve to motivate a new generation of entrepreneurs to build fundamentally better, more nimble and customer-oriented institutions.reply

Railroads, semiconductors, plastics, networking... the utility was there for all of them, and so was the potential profit.Everybody knew it.But some investors don't have the patience for these "sure things" to mature into their commercial destiny and others know they can siphon off a killing by taking advantage of them as they speculate.These bubbles aren't about potential, they're about timing.And today's AI, for as revolutionary as it may be, is taking just as long to mature as anything in the past.Most of the top players involved in AI right now are going to be rich. And in 20 years, the world is going to involve a lot of AI in soooo many things. But a lot of shirts are going to be lost below those top players and a lot of companies are going to fold because infrastructure, refinement, and integration take time while the FOMO speculation starts as soon as the big discovery is recognized.reply

> Railroads, semiconductors, plastics, networking... the utility was there for all of them, and so was the potential profit.Canals... where a repeating pattern was the company underestimating difficulty/costs, and going unrecoverably into debt. Another company, which then bought the largely finished canal, cheap, they had potential profit... until tech change (railroads).reply
Capital cycle theory: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2J2Fb1bBufA&t=577sreply

I just wish we lived in a world without the speculative bubbles, because if this had been developed slowly, deliberately, over time, there would be no necessity to cast aside troublesome details like safety, suitability, and ethics...and we could enjoy the fruits as it was implemented gradually, responsibly, as it matures. As opposed to going "wow, this is really cool, but gosh I feel shitty about using it..."Nor would it have been thrust blindly into the hands of your manager, the marketing department, the CEO, and countless other folks who have no understanding of how it works, its limitations, or its risks.reply

The difference is that all those things needed physical infrastructure to be linearly build out.AI models can be deployed on the same datacenter as the old one and be either orders of magnitude cheaper to run, or orders of magnitude more capable.The only thing that can pop this bubble is if we're not smart enough.reply

This reads less like a bulwark against sensationalism and more like an attempt to remain ideologically safe in what appears from many angles to be an extremely steep exponential start of what we can probably agree is an S-curve.> And today's AI, for as revolutionary as it may be, is taking just as long to mature as anything in the past.I suspect this opinion may come across as naive for the myriad software engineers whose job has become pressing the enter key. Your point about timing is based on solid principles, but I don't think your comment contains a satisfactory argument that the timing is incorrect.reply

How do you know we aren't already through the exponential part of the S-curve and about to enter the AGI winter (i.e. AGI will require a fundamentally different technology than LLMs that is still decades off)?If no one is willing to pay increasingly high costs of training frontier models, we'll still have the models that we have now that can be fine tuned for incremental improvements. title: Declarative Dragging (declarative-dragging.github.io)
comments: Funny story about drag-and-drop:At my very first job, we had a weekly meeting to assign tickets and estimates.Our non-technical PM wrote "drag-and-drop" on a whiteboard, and then my name."Gavin, how long do you think this will take?""All week. At least. Maybe longer?"PM laughed, then realized I wasn't making a joke."What do you mean 'all week'? That's ridiculous, do I need to give this to someone else?""Well, you could, but I wouldn't count on you getting it any sooner."Appalled, he exclaims: "It's just drag-and-drop!"After 10-15 minutes of a room full of engineers trying to explain the difficulty, he gave up with an unhappy "Fine."The phrase "it's just drag-and-drop" became an inside joke for the rest of my time there...reply
I think non-tech people think that drag and drop is some sort of emergent property because you're pressing the mouse and holding it pressed.reply
Dumb question: why? It’s been a long time since I touched GUI code, but I thought it gave you a message with the URI to the file. How is this significantly different than file-open?reply

This was circa 2010 or so, and it was a web app. So pre-ES6 JavaScript, before React.Nowadays you would just "npm install drag-and-drop" but back then you often had to hand-roll solutions.If anyone can dig up an ancient library on GitHub for drag-and-drop back in those days, I'd imagine it would be several thousand lines long, not to mention the absolute nightmare that testing something like this with a proper framework and accompanying testing library.reply
Ah, I was thinking desktop applications.reply

Hit-test where the mouse-down event is fired, hit-test where the mouse-up event is fired. What the hell do you need a library for?> If anyone can dig up an ancient library on GitHub for drag-and-drop back in those days, I'd imagine it would be several thousand lines long,I bet, the JS devs who do write code overcompensate for the ones who can only stitch together libraries. I suppose because the expectation is that the library consumer is incapable of writing their own code extending it, so the library itself must support every possible combination of use cases for a million different users, even though the code any individual consumer actually needs is more like 100 loc.reply

> What the hell do you need a library for?

On the frontend, you have to re-calculate the display state for all the possible drop positions, in-between transitions, and drop-end-snap-back.Think of a grid of cards, and all the possible drag, hover, and drop state transitions it can be in with any other card, and the animations required to make it look niceNow also consider that you need to persist the final state on the backend, and handle things like rejection, cancellation, failed updates/errors.It becomes a massive state chart and web of complexityreply

I mean, maybe we're missing context here. Is that what your boss was actually asking for? 99% of web applications (or, hell, desktop applications) don't have ultra-interactive, fully-responsive-animation drag-and-drop. If he was asking for functional drag-and-drop and the team was implementing top 1% cosmetic drag-and-drop, that's certainly one avenue for a mismatch in expectations.reply

What does that look like mid drag, and how?If you are dragging within the page, then the draggable “ghost” is your problem too (it’s not automatic). As is deciding whether the ghost should affirmatively snap out of and into the source and target containers (that is, whether the destination container should appear to “make room” for the ghost at some transitional point), whether there’s a transition on that, etc.Drag and drop in desktop non-web GUIs have all sorts of visual affordances that users expect for consistency that are your job in HTML.I was once quite up-to-date with raw frontend work and I tried to implement this; it’s actually not trivial.reply

> draggable ghostOkay, you've added a requirement. Poll the current cursor position after the first hit-test sets the dragging state and call a function to render your object with X% opacity at a higher Z level than anything else. Your 30 minute job has become a 60 minute job.> As is deciding whether the ghost should affirmatively snap out of and into the source and target containers (that is, whether the destination container should appear to “make room” for the ghost at some point), whether there’s a transition on that,Most applications don't go this far, including your operating system like Windows that sets baseline UX expectations, so you're well beyond the default expectation for drag-and-drop. If someone asks you to implement drag-and-drop without specifying they want all the bells and whistles, and you respond it's going to take you a week because you're planning to go all-out beyond necessary business requirements, they'd have a valid reason to be like "WTF mate?". Also this is still pretty paltry and not a week's worth of work.reply

Joshua Horowitz,
      Andrew Blinn,

What if making a diagram draggable was as simple as specifying what it can become?
        Drag-and-drop makes the digital graspable. But designing bespoke drag interactions involves a lot of fiddly code to
        handle geometry, feedback, and animations. As a result, many people, from educators to game designers,
        mathematicians to creative tool builders, often don't bother.
      
Declarative dragging inverts the problem. Rather than programming all that visual behavior directly, you
        simply say, for each element you want to make draggable, which future states of your application dragging it
        should lead to. Our system speculatively renders those states to work
        out where things can go, then combines these possible worlds into a smooth, responsive drag-and-drop
        interaction.

title: A Bit about Email (maurycyz.com)
comments: xxx
first_paragraph:
First, some terminology;
A typical email will past through many different components on the way to the recipient: 


(These aren't all necessarily different machines or even different programs, but it is helpful to name each step.)

The mail user agent (MUA) runs on the user's computer and is what they use to send or read messages.
Let's say they send something:
that message will be uploaded to to the submission agent (MSA) which checks the user's password before handing off to the mail transfer agent (MTA).

The transfer agent's job is to talk to other mail servers and get the message to the receiving side's MTA.
Once received, it's given to the local delivery agent (LDA) to be stored until the recipient checks their email.
The name "LDA" is non-standard, but I use it to avoid having four different abbreviations differing by a single letter.

The reason for this structure is that when the system was being designed (around 1980),
most organizations could only afford a single server.

title: Ask HN: How do you manage your AI agents' context across clients and projects?
comments: As many have said - my strong steer build something[^1].There are _great_ tools for this, but the biggest part of this is managing your own attention, and mental load. You can craft something that really helps _you_ manage all the spinning plates.In the case of my harness, I hoover up all the PR state into one place and then have a bunch of rules on how I interact with them (or not). Even down to a "swipe right to merge" card system. Works for me.My recommendation: A cloudflare PWA fully vibe coded with zerotrust on the front. Don't get too attached, tools are changing fast. Make it work and be prepared to ditch it when something better comes along.[1] https://jonathannen.com/build-your-own-lightsaber/reply

It seems many have built similar tools for solving this.Mine lets me run Claude and Codex (and pi but then you have to pay API rates) from the same localhosted webserver, and also schedule feature implementations to always hit the weekly usage cap. chats logs in jsonl (used by both) are saved per project in a never-pushed git branch. All agents run in Podman containers.I am just starting to play with a higher-level agent that just pushes the repo in a direction based on the human answering a thorough list of clarification questions.These have been really useful- Encourage short, commit-linked chats, to avoid the expensive cache writes.- Plot of LOC over time. Use better models until this starts not spiking a ton with every new feature.- Terminals kinda suck for agentic stuff IMO and we should stop cramming agent loops into them. Minimalism doesn't really help here, it's really nice to have built-in STT, real buttons, easy scrolling, etc etc etc.- The minimal delta is a commit. Every implementation turn must end with one or multiple, and a clean worktree.- Crystal clear, extremely granular usage data. This is something Claude Code and Codex will never give you, instead you get dark patterns nudging you to forget about the spend, while changing plan quotas every couple weeks.reply

When I start a new project, I point to other ones where I'm happy with the quality as exemplars. I think its probably simpler to copy relevant stuff allow older projects go out of date until I start working on them again, then I tell the agent to look at the newer project to update its style.I have 2-4 on going projects I tend to a bit of that, normally 2 at a time, when I pick up one of the others, I really just do that; point to the older one.But within projects I don't really try to manage context, more so I just have an issue tracker which I add to keep track of stuff. In 2 of my long running projects I have some bootleg issue tracker built in (along with a screenshot QA tool which sends issues to the tracker) into the UI of the tool.I guess to extent I can, I try to avoid keeping some preferences in the context like formatting and linting (including directory structure and white listing imports in certain parts). I've been trying to find more ways to automate that way, so I keep my prompts and skills and goals limited to objectives where possible, so preferences like styles and structure are automatically enforced.When I have multiple agents, I just tell them to maintain write only ledgers to coordinate to avoid overlapping work, but it's easier when your project is broken up into self contained components with communication boundaries (defined in protobuf) like a FE/BE split or seperate service codebases (I reassemble it as a google style modular monolith to avoid running too many processes)reply

I built a tool for myself for this. It runs on localhost and uses sqlite as a storage engine for metadata, and the XDG paradigm for content (eg ~/.local/share, ~/.local/state) I create topics, eg localhost:8080/topic/1. Each topic can have tickets, artifacts and sessions. Tickets are linked task tracking tickets (eg Jira, though not actually Jira in my case), artifacts are documents etc produced during sessions, and sessions are Claude Code sessions (though it wouldn't have to be Claude, that's just what I use).Sessions run in a terminal emulator in the browser. What makes this work is that I have some general purpose directions/context each topic gets, but there's also a running topic.md that gets updated at the end of each session. This way my context builds up and persists specific to that topic. Artifacts the agent produces (eg specs, plans) open up in a sidebar and render as HTML even though they're stored as markdown, and its easy to go back and find them from previous sessions. Session transcripts also are accessible from the Topic page.I do regularly run compaction on the topic.md, moving the full content to an archive and keeping the working context smaller.reply

Karpathys LLM wiki with QMD.I have a small gatekeeper.py script the agent has to run to complete a round or begin a new one. One of the things it does (in addition to record keeping, linting, etc) is validate that the wiki has been updated with all the findings, lessons learned, and documentation for the round. The agent can't proceed until it's done.Then in the AGENTS.md they're told they can use QMD to perform semantic search of the wiki , and should before starting any significant work.It's expensive, in terms of tokens, but well worth it. I could reproduce any stage of my project if I wanted. I always know why they did what they did (if they do), and the agent's can't really forget anything important.reply
